topic.name: Calculating Volumes of Solids Using Triple Integrals

question.text:
Find the volume of the solid region above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.
question.explanation:
Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

\[ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 2+y-z \big\}, \]

where

\[ D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2 \big\} \]

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

Hence, the type II representation of $R$ is

\[ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 3, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 2+y-z \big\}. \]

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

\begin{align*} V &= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{2+y-z} \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{2} \big[ x \big]_{x=0}^{x=2+y-z} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{2} (2+y-z)-0 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{2} 2+y-z \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \left[ (2+y)z-\dfrac{z^2}{2} \right]_{z=0}^{z=2} \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} \left( (2+y)(2)-\dfrac{2^2}{2} \right) - 0 \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{3} 2 + 2y \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \big[ 2y + y^2 \big]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\[5pt] &= (2(3) + 3^2) - 0 \\[5pt] &= 15. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Given a Diagram

question.text: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $yz$-plane, the surface $x=6yz+12,$ and the planes $y=0,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$
question.explanation:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region:

\[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 6yz+12 \right\} \]

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

\begin{align*} V &= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{6yz+12} \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} \big[ x \big]_{x=0}^{x=6yz+12} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} (6yz+12) - 0 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} 6yz+12 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \big[ 3yz^2+12z \big]_{z=0}^{z=1} \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \left( 3y(1)^2+12(1) \right) - 0 \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} 3y+12 \: \mathrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{3}{2}y^2+12y \right]_{y=0}^{y=2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} (2^2-0) + 12(2-0) \\[5pt] &= 30. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Given a Description

question.text: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xz$-plane and the surface $y = 5-3z^2,$ and the planes $x = 0,$ $x = 1,$ $z = -1,$ $z = 0.$
question.explanation:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: \[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: -1 \leq z \leq 0, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 5-3z^2 \right\} \]

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral: \begin{align*} V & = \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{-1}^{0} \int_{0}^{5-3z^2} \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{-1}^{0} \big[ y \big]_{y=0}^{y=5-3z^2} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{-1}^{0} 5-3z^2 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \big[5z - z^3\big]_{z=-1}^{z=0} \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} 0-(5(-1) - (-1)^3) \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} 5 - 1 \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 4\int_{0}^{1} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 4\big[ x \big]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= 4(1-0) \\[5pt] & = 4 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Given a Description

question.text: Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloid $x=-2+y^2+4z^2$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=-1+2z^2,$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows: \[ \displaystyle V = \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{a(y)}}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{b(y)}} \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{f(y,z)} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \] What is $a^2+b^2+f?$
question.explanation:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

\begin{align*} -2+y^2+4z^2 &=-1+2z^2 \\[3pt] y^2+2z^2 &= 1 \\[3pt] y^2+2z^2 &= 1 \end{align*}

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region:

\[ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: -2+y^2+4z^2 \leq x \leq -1+2z^2 \big\}, \]

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $y^2+2z^2 = 1.$

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by

\begin{align*} V &= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{-2+y^2+4z^2}^{-1+2z^2} \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{D} (-1+2z^2) - (-2+y^2+4z^2) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{D} 1 - y^2 - 2 z^2 \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of

  • the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\dfrac{1-y^2}{2}},$ and

  • the upper part $z=\sqrt{\dfrac{1-y^2}{2}},$

for $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D} 1 - y^2 - 2 z^2 \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{\color{red}-\sqrt{(1-y^2)/2}}^{\color{red}\sqrt{(1-y^2)/2}} \: {\color{blue} 1 - y^2 - 2 z^2} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y. \end{align*}

Finally,

\begin{align*} a^2+b^2+f &= \left(-\sqrt{\dfrac{1-y^2}{2}}\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1-y^2}{2}}\right)^2 + \left(1 - y^2 - 2z^2\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1-y^2}2 + \dfrac{1-y^2}2 + (1 - y^2 - 2 z^2) \\[5pt] &=2 - 2y^2 - 2 z^2. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume

question.text:
Find the volume of the solid region above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.
question.explanation:
Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

\[ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 4-2x-4z \big\}, \]

where $D$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane.

To find the top boundary curve of $D$ in the form $z=z(x),$ we substitute $y=0$ into the equation $y=4-2x-4z{:}$

\[ 0=4-2x-4z \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad z=1-\dfrac{x}{2} \]

Then, we have \[ D = \left\{ (x,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1-\dfrac{x}2 \right\}, \] as shown below.

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

\[ R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1-\dfrac{x}2, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 4-2x-4z \big\}. \]

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

\begin{align*} V &= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1-x/2} \int_{0}^{4-2x-4z} \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1-x/2} \big[ y \big]_{y=0}^{y=4-2x-4z} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1-x/2} (4-2x-4z)-0 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1-x/2} 4-2x-4z \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \left[ (4-2x)z - 2z^2 \right]_{z=0}^{z=1-x/2} \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \left( (4-2x)\left(1-\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - 2\left(1-\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 \right) - 0 \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \left(1-\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\left( (4-2x) - 2\left(1-\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \right) \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac12\left(2-x\right)\left(2-x\right) \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} 2 - 2x + \dfrac{x^2}{2} \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ 2x - x^2 + \dfrac{x^3}{6} \right]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\[5pt] &= \left(2(2) - 2^2 + \dfrac{2^3}{6} \right) - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac43. \end{align*}
